la:noun:cacumen.html:
căcūmen, ĭnis, n.
etym. dub.
,
the extreme end, extremity, or point of a thing; the peak, top, utmost point.
Lit. (whether horizontal or perpendicular; while culmen is an extremity projecting in height; v. Doed. Syn.; in the poets freq.; in prose rare before the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): ut altis Arboribus vicina cacumina summa terantur Inter se,the extreme top,. —So of tree-tops: umbrosa cacumina,: fracta,; 6, 28; ; ; ; ; ; 8, 257; 8, 716; 8, 756; 9, 389; 10, 140; 10, 193; 13, 833; 15, 396; ; : arborum cacumina,: ficorum, pirorum, malorum,: olivae, and 15; 11, 3, 37; ; ; ; ; ; : harundinis,.—Of grass, the points of the blades, : praeacutis (ramorum) cacuminibus,; .— Of the summits, peaks of mountains, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 6, 311; 8, 797; 7, 804; 9, 93; , ; —Of other things: pilorum, Auct. B. Afr. 47: atomi,: cujusque rei,: ovi,; . 54, 75, § 151: metae,: pyramidis,: membrorum,. 88, § 219: ignis,: incurvum, of the elephant's back,.—
Trop.
The end, limit: donec alescundi summum tetigere cacumen, until they have completely attained the limit of their growth, : ad summum donec venere cacumen,to the height of perfection,: famae, Laber. ap. .—
As a gram. t. t., the mark of accent placed over a letter, .

la:noun:cacus.html:
Cācus, i, m., = Κᾶκος,
son of Vulcan, contemporary with Evander, a giant of immense physical strength, who dwelt in a cave on Mount Aventinus, and troubled the whole region around by his robberies; he robbed even Hercules of the cattle of Geryon, and was on that account slain by him, ; ; , and Serv. in h. l.; ; 4 (5), 9, 16; ; ; , §§ 7 and 18.

la:other:Cacus.gloss: A fire-breathing giant and son of Vulcan, who was killed by Hercules.

senses: to laugh loudly or immoderately; to cachinnate
la:verb:cachinno.html:
căchinno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n.
like καχάζω or καγχάζω; Sanscr. kakk; and our titter, onomatop.
,
to laugh aloud, laugh immoderately.
Lit. (class. but rare): famulae furtim cachinnant,; ; : ridere convivae; cachinnare ipse Apronius,; ; .—With the acc. of that which one laughs at: exitum meum cachinnant,.—*
Poet. (v. Liddell and Scott under καχλάζω, γέλως, γέλασμα, and Blomfield. Aesch. Prom. 90) of the sea, to plash, ripple, roar: suavisona echo crepitu clangente cachinnat, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 572 Rib.).

la:noun:cachinnus.html:
căchinnus, i, m.
id.
,
a loud laugh, immoderate laughter, a laugh in derision, a jeering.
Lit. (class in prose and poetry; also in plur.): tum dulces esse cachinni consuerant,; so : in quo Alcibiades cachinnum dicitur sustulisse,to have set up a loud laugh,; : tollere,: cachinnos irridentium commovere,: res digna tuo cachinno,; ; : securus,: perversus,: major,; : rigidus,: temulus,: effusus in cachinnos,: cachinnum edere,: cachinnos revocare,.—*
Poet., of the sea (cf. 1, cachinno, II.), a plashing, rippling, roaring: leni resonant plangore cachinni, (cf. Aesch. Prom. 90' ποντίων τε κυμάτων ὐνήριθμον γέλασμα).
